articles.title: Near-Death Experiences and Near-Death-Like Experiences: A Comparative Synthesis and Implications for Their Interpretation
articles.authors: Patrizio Tressoldi
articles.abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are most often reported in association with physiologically life-threatening events such as cardiac arrest or coma, but phenomenologically similar reports, near-death-like (NDE-like) experiences, also arise in the absence of a life threat, for example during syncope, deep meditation, hypnosis, and psychedelic states. This synthesis reviews the evidence on whether the phenomenology, psychological correlates, and aftereffects of NDEs differ from those of NDE-like experiences. Comparing the largest retrospective survey, a mixed-methods online study, and a within-person psychedelic comparison, consistently indicate broad overlap in core features across contexts. At the same time, encounters with deceased persons or spiritual entities were reported in 34.7% NDE accounts and none of 25 NDE-like accounts in one exploratory study, and a single-case comparison found life review, encounters with the deceased, and a threshold or point of no return present only in the NDE. However, no study was designed to test equivalence, samples were largely self-selected and retrospective, and formal measurement-invariance testing of the instruments in use across etiologies is still lacking. These constraints caution against concluding phenomenological identity. The implications of this evidence for neurophysiological, psychological, evolutionary, and metaphysical interpretations are analyzed, and priorities for prospective, preregistered, adequately powered research are outlined.

articles.title: Imagining Oneself or the Object? Task-Dependent Effects in Mental Paper Folding and Body Rotation
articles.authors: Stephan Frederic Dahm; Carla Czilczer; Marcos Moreno-Verdú; Pierre Sachse
articles.abstract: While theoretical accounts of action imagery emphasize the role of the actor performing the movement, it remains unclear whether self-related kinesthetic imagery (self-imagery) compared to object-related visual imagery (object-imagery) supports mental transformations similarly for body-related and non-body stimuli. To clarify this relationship, 142 participants completed the mental paper folding task and the mental body rotation task under two imagery instructions: based on self-imagery or object-imagery. Instructions successfully shifted subjective imagery experiences, with self-imagery emphasizing bodily sensations and object-imagery emphasizing visualization. Performance analyses revealed robust task-specific effects: mental paper folding performance decreased with the number of folds and direction changes, and mental body rotation performance decreased for larger (than smaller) rotations, for front-view (than back-view) stimuli and for foot (than hand) stimuli. Crucially, errors did not significantly differ between imagery instructions. For response times, however, the relative advantage of the instructions was task-specific. Response times were shorter under self-imagery in mental body rotations but shorter under object-imagery in mental paper folding. Yet, in mental paper folding, this effect varied with instruction order, which might reflect a carryover effect of self-referential processing from self-imagery to object-imagery. Cross-task response times resulted in medium correlations when imagery instructions matched, whereas error rate correlations showed no consistent pattern. Overall, the findings indicate that the advantage of self-imagery versus object-imagery depends on task demands. They are consistent with flexible recruitment of imagery processes, while leaving open whether this reflects different configurations of a shared system or partly distinct motor and visuospatial strategies.

articles.title: Building the future: Schemas contribute to episodic simulation
articles.authors: Sabrina Laurenne Valenzano; Isaac Kinley; Reece Pierre Roberts; Daniel L Schacter; Donna Rose Addis
articles.abstract: Future imagination is argued to rely on schematic knowledge and executive functions, yet direct evidence is lacking. Participants (N=50) completed executive measures and imagined future events involving schema-congruent or -incongruent objects and locations. Events were rated for detail and plausibility and scored for episodic content. We also collected descriptions of the locations in a separate sample (N=20) that served as proxies for culturally-shared schemas in a narrative representational similarity analysis (RSA): schema and event texts were converted into high-dimensional vectors using document embeddings, and cosine similarity was computed between vectors. RSA showed evidence of schema use: event narratives were most similar in meaning to schema descriptions of the same locations, particularly at the start of trials. Executive capacities were unrelated to schema use, although relational reasoning ability was associated with higher subjective detail on congruent trials. This study provides initial direct evidence of schema use in service of future imagining.

articles.title: Particularized Truth and Reality Testing in the Algorithmic Era
articles.authors: Daniela Ben Zeev; Dror Oren
articles.abstract:
How can two individuals posing the same question to a conversational model receive different answers, and what are the implications for our understanding of truth and reality testing? The human search for truth has taken various forms: truth as revealed, investigated through science, encountered psychologically, and, today, approached through probability and computation. We distinguish between truth, relative truth, and reality testing, proposing that reality testing relies on an “outside” grounded in objective criteria. Yet conversational models do not merely retrieve information; they formulate a representation of reality within an encounter with a specific inquirer. The user’s input and history participate in shaping the response, such that the “outside” returns tailored to their world. The novelty lies not in algorithmic mediation as such, but in the structural shift in the relationship between subject, representation, and outside.
We propose the concept of Particularized Truth: neither a new ontological category nor a mere adjustment of style, but a form in which a claim about reality becomes present for a specific subject within an algorithmic encounter, influencing content and recommendations. Research on sycophancy provides empirical support for aspects of this adaptive process. Under some conditions, such adaptation may shift the interaction from the demands of the reality principle toward the pleasure principle—the wish that the world offer no resistance. We therefore propose an expansion of reality testing in the AI era, examining how representations are generated and their capacity to diverge from the user’s existing perspective. Reality testing requires an outside, even when the outside has learned to speak our language.

articles.title: Striking the Limits of the Rich-Get-Richer and the Poor-Get-Richer Hypothesis?  Trait Interpersonal Emotion Regulation and its Associations with Instant Messaging Emotional Support and Mental Health in Daily Life
articles.authors: Karen De Raeymaecker; Imke Baetens; Margot Bastin; Martijn Van Heel
articles.abstract: Up until now, the role of dispositions in the psychosocial effects of adolescent instant messaging (IM) remains inconclusive. While the straightforward rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer hypotheses do not allow for nuances about the individual-specific (dis)advantages of offline and online interactions, the literature on the dispositional tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation shows a more complex picture. In this ecological momentary study (one week, 8 assessments/day), we adopted the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer framework to test the social and psychological effects of IM with regard to the dispositional tendencies for co-rumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing in 181 Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women). Adolescents with a higher tendency for co-dampening reported lower mean levels of momentary positive affect. Individuals with a clear tendency for co-enhancing experienced, on average, higher momentary IM emotional support. Regarding the tendency for co-rumination, no significant differences were found. Notably, (dis)advantageous social effects did not go together with similar psychological effects. Unexpectedly, IM behaviors (e.g., IM negative social exchange) were, regardless of the studied outcome and the level of analysis, systematically significant. Overall, this study endorses the importance of the abovementioned dispositional tendencies. Yet, their value was more limited than the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses predicted.

articles.title: Owning the Gap: How Observers Judge the Distance Between What People Say They Want and What They Do
articles.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles.abstract: Observers evaluate more than what people achieve. They also evaluate how people stand toward the distance between an aspiration and their conduct. This paper proposes gap ownership as a construct for that stance. It follows Weber's ideal-type method as extended by Etzrodt. Three types are derived from two questions: whether the aspiration is kept, and whether the actor accepts authorship of the gap. In the owned gap, the actor answers for the distance. In the disowned gap, the actor keeps the aspiration, does not live it, and places its failure outside the self. In the dissolved gap, each aspiration is replaced before it is acted on. The last two correspond to the alienation and anomie poles in Etzrodt's reading of Weber. For a fixed gap, observers' respect, irritation, contempt, and discounting are predicted to depend on the stance, whatever the desirability of the aspiration. The claim has a domain. For obligations to others, a good excuse softens the listener. For self-regarding aspirations the paper predicts the reverse: answering for the gap earns more respect than explaining it away. Seven propositions carry refutation conditions, and rival predictions separate ownership from behavioral integrity, false signaling, listener burden, and the controllability of excuses.

articles.title: A Momentary Goldilocks Story?  Adolescent Dispositional Traits and their Relationship with Momentary Instant Messaging Social Support and Mental Health
articles.authors: Karen De Raeymaecker; Imke Baetens; Glenn Kiekens; Martijn Van Heel
articles.abstract: Despite the heightened need of connectedness in adolescence, the association between instant messaging (IM) and its psychosocial outcomes remains ambiguous. In line with three existing theories on this topic, ecological momentary assessment (one week, 8 prompts/day) was used to link within-person IM behavior and between-person dispositions with the social outcome perceived IM social support and the psychological outcomes loneliness, depressive feelings, and non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) behavior. Furthermore, the interplay between the two was taken into account. Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women) who reported higher-than-usual IM connection behavior consistently showed better momentary psychosocial outcomes. Robust differences related to the dispositions could only be identified for depressive feelings. Women and participants with higher scores on neuroticism, fear of negative evaluation, social anxiety and distress in new situations, and social comparison orientation proved more vulnerable for these feelings. A tentative association related to loneliness was found for higher neuroticism. Moreover, age (marginally) strengthened the negative association between IM behavior and the outcomes IM social support and depressive feelings. In general, these findings highlight the importance of the perceived message content, the  potential vulnerability of more extreme dispositions, and the value of embedding psychosocial correlates in a developmental framework.

articles.title: Fast Eyes, Sharp Eyes, or Good Eyes? What Links Visual Perception to Higher-Order Cognition
articles.authors: Shanglin Yang; Rean Du; Jeffrey N. Rouder
articles.abstract: Why do simple perceptual tasks predict higher-order cognition, such as working memory and fluid intelligence? We contrast three hypotheses. Fast eyes: individuals who extract visual information quickly do well on both perceptual and cognitive tasks. Sharp eyes: individuals who resolve targets clearly in visual noise do well on both. Good eyes: a general visual ability, specific to neither speed nor noise, underlies both. To distinguish them, we crossed three stimulus types (Pi, letter, Gabor) with two masking types. In temporal masking, a mask follows the target and limits processing time; in spatial masking, the same mask accompanies the target and limits visibility through noise. Each task’s temporal and spatial versions thus shared the same stimulus and mask, differing only in how the mask was presented. 79 participants completed these perceptual tasks and four cognitive tasks. A hierarchical psychometric structural equation model decomposed individual differences into general visual, masking, and stimulus factors and related each to cognitive performance. The results show that masking type accounted for relatively little variance and was unrelated to cognitive performance. Stimulus type accounted for more variance but was also unrelated to cognitive performance. Only the general visual factor, shared across all perceptual tasks, was strongly related to cognitive performance (*r* = .64), supporting the good-eyes hypothesis.

articles.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
articles.authors: Robert Nosofsky; Adam F Osth
articles.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.  However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.  Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.  Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.  Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.  The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

articles.title: Navigating Safety in Reproductive Health Self-Care Interventions in Ghana: A Qualitative Study
articles.authors: Kwasi Adu Manu; Sarah E. Stutterheim; Charles Adjei; Francine Schneider
articles.abstract:
Introduction
Reproductive health self-care interventions are growing rapidly in Ghana, but there is limited evidence on the quality-of-care provisions that ensure safety for end-users and health professionals. This study explored how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, using a self-care-specific conceptual framework.

Materials and Methods
Using an exploratory qualitative approach, underpinned by the Quality-of-Care Framework for Self-Care, we interviewed 29 end-users and 19 professionals, comprising health providers, program managers, digital referral agents, and community facilitators across Accra, Tamale, Cape Coast, and Sunyani. The study spanned six sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) domains: family planning, abortion, HIV/STI, maternal and child health, general SRHR, and cervical cancer. Data was analysed using thematic analysis techniques in Dedoose, grounded in both deductive and inductive principles.

Results
Key outcomes include the following: Technical Competency – Despite barriers, end-users felt sufficiently empowered to access self-care services. although professionals required continuous capacity strengthening to keep pace with the evolving ecosystem; Client Safety – End-users preferred access to medical eligibility information, but professionals were while professionals expressed concerns about potential misuse; Information Exchange – Information on family planning self-care services was more openly available than across other SRHR domains; Interpersonal Connection and Choice – End-users reported more positive experiences with remote services than facility-based care, although professionals faced operational constraints that affected consistent delivery of quality care; Continuity of Care – Follow-up care was better integrated across health facilities than alternate service delivery points, with periodic stockouts disrupting continuity efforts.

Conclusion
In exploring how quality of care and safety are experienced and maintained within reproductive health self-care interventions in Ghana, this study found that end-users and professionals have adopted interim measures to maintain some level of safety amid policy and institutional inadequacies. However, the sustainability of these measures is uncertain, posing a serious risk to public health if not prioritised in the short term.

articles.title: Building Connection Through Conversation: Linguistic Convergence and Neural Complexity in Dyadic Interaction
articles.authors: Grace Qiyuan Miao; Zachary P Rosen; Agnieszka Pluta; MATTHEW D. LIEBERMAN; Rick Dale; Yuwei Li
articles.abstract: Interpersonal connection emerges through conversation. Theories of interpersonal communication hold that conversational partners increasingly align in how they express meaning, build on one another’s contributions, and experience connection. Yet how such alignment unfolds during a conversation, and how it relates to the experience of a “good” interaction, remains largely untested. Seventy dyads of previously unacquainted individuals held naturalistic conversations while dual functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) recorded neural activity. We measured semantic alignment using convergence entropy and substantive exchange, the number of adjacent turns in which both partners contributed contentful talk. Contrary to a convergence account, dyads broadened their semantic range over time. Subjective experience was predicted not by semantic alignment but by substantive exchange, particularly in shallow-prompt conversations. Neurally, inter-brain synchrony tracked substantive exchange, whereas semantic alignment was reflected in partners’ matched turn-to-turn neural dynamics. First conversations build connection through reciprocal, substantive exchange, with distinct linguistic and neural signatures.

articles.title: Effects of active learning and talker variability on preschoolers' novel word learning
articles.authors: Federica Bulgarelli; Marina Rabideau
articles.abstract: Words sound different every time they are said, both by the same person and across people. This variability has been found to have mixed effects on learning. For example, 14-month-olds benefit from talker variability when learning minimal pairs, but struggle when learning distinct-sounding words. Talker variability is found to be particularly beneficial for learning to produce novel words. All of these previous studies have used passive exposure, presenting participants with predetermined orders or fixed types of variability. Here, we used an active learning paradigm wherein preschoolers could choose who to hear words from during word learning. Then, we tested whether participants seek out variability during word learning, how these talker variability choices influence word learning and whether actively making these choices results in different outcomes than passively receiving them. We find that preschoolers choose to hear words from multiple talkers, and talker variability choices interact with active learning to predict production, but not comprehension. Taken together, our results suggest that preschool aged children can make choices are benefit their own learning, informing theories of both talker variability and active learning.

articles.title: What Are Situationships? Characteristics of an Ambiguous Relationship Type
articles.authors: Saffron Marli Costello; William Costello; Andrew G. Thomas; Martin Graff
articles.abstract:
Situationships are an emerging relationship type, yet quantitative research remains limited. Here we examined situationship characteristics and experiences, using sex and sociosexuality as theoretically relevant starting points for understanding individual variation. We conducted an exploratory, cross-sectional survey of 390 adults (68% women; M age = 27.41 years, SD = 8.66) from 48 countries who reported on current, or emotionally significant past, situationships. Participants endorsed proposed situationship characteristics and provided their own open-ended definitions which underwent structured content coding. These analyses informed a working definition of situationships as intimate, relationship-like connections lacking clarity about commitment, relationship status, or future trajectory. Although 56% of participants entered situationships hoping for a relationship, and 55% assumed sexual exclusivity, only 9% of reported past situationships progressed to a committed relationship. Compared with men, women more often emphasised ambiguity in their definitions, perceived greater long-term potential, and expressed stronger hopes for commitment. They also more strongly agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner saw other people. Relative to the reference sample, both sexes reported more unrestricted sociosexual behaviour, whereas women reported more restricted sociosexual attitudes. This pattern raises questions about incongruence between women’s sexual experiences and preferences, with potential implications for wellbeing. The observed sex differences also motivate future research to examine whether divergent mating goals between partners shape situationship experiences.
Keywords: situationships, romantic relationships, sex differences, sociosexuality

articles.title: Factor Structure of the Auditory-Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire  and Development of a Brief Scale
articles.authors: Zach Hambrick; Elizabeth S. Eberlin; Katharine N. Thakkar
articles.abstract: Nikitova and colleagues’ Auditory and Visual Abnormalities Questionnaire (AVAQ) is the first comprehensive assessment of the type of perceptual abnormalities associated with the schizophrenia spectrum (Nikitova et al., 2019). The primary aim of this study was to investigate the factor structure of the AVAQ and develop a brief version of the scale. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated that the AVAQ is multidimensional, capturing a general factor of perceptual abnormalities, along with more specific types of perceptual abnormalities. Through item-level analyses, we identified 23 items that capture this factor structure. A Brief AVAQ scale consisting of these 23 items exhibited good reliability and convergent validity in two relatively large samples. This scale could be used in both research and clinical practice.

articles.title: The Governed Heart:  Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy
articles.authors: Nicholas Paul Camp; Brett Quaid Ford
articles.abstract: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone. Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents. We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions. Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings. We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means. We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation – targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses – with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people’s environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization. Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.

articles.title: Long-Term Predictors of Word Reading Fluency Beyond the Early Elementary Grades
articles.authors: Maria Psyridou; KATERINA KATOPODI; George K. Georgiou; Athanassios Protopapas
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Word reading fluency continues to develop after accuracy is achieved, yet which early skills drive this development beyond earlier attainment remains unclear. We examined the longitudinal development of word reading fluency in Greek from Grade 2 to 6 to find out (1) how stable fluency is across these grades, (2) which early cognitive and linguistic skills predict Grade 6 fluency beyond prior attainment, and (3) whether the suppression effects commonly reported in concurrent designs hold longitudinally.
Method: Greek children (n = 268) were assessed at the beginning of Grade 2 on serial and discrete naming (digits, objects, words, pseudowords), phonological awareness, orthographic knowledge, articulation rate, morphological awareness, vocabulary, and nonverbal ability, and on word reading fluency at the end of Grades 2, 3, and 6. Longitudinal structural equation models with autoregressive paths were used to identify unique predictors. 
Results: Fluency was highly stable (β = .88 from Grade 2 to 3; β = .64 from Grade 3 to 6). Grade 2 fluency was predicted mainly by discrete word naming. Beyond Grade 3 fluency, serial digit naming, orthographic knowledge, and articulation rate predicted Grade 6 fluency, accounting for an additional 13% of the variance, but only when discrete digit naming was included as a suppressor. General cognitive and linguistic measures made no contribution.
Conclusions: The predictors of word reading fluency appear to change across the primary school years, from word-level naming to sequential processing, orthographic knowledge, and articulatory speed. Word reading fluency may thus be better understood not as a unitary skill that simply improves quantitatively over time, but as a developmentally shifting construct.

articles.title: Own and others' confidence in social information use
articles.authors: Andrea Gradassi; Wouter van den Bos; Lucas Molleman
articles.abstract: The behaviour of friends, colleagues, television hosts and social media feeds affects what we buy, how we dress, and who we vote for. People tend to be more sensitive to social influence when unsure about their beliefs and when the source is highly confident. Less is known about the relative impact of the confidence of self and others’ on social information use, and how they jointly shape social transmission. We present results of two incentivized decision-making tasks (N=203 and N=213, samples from the U.S.A.) where participants could adjust their initial estimates upon observing estimates of peers and their confidence. Adjustments were most sensitive to the confidence of others when participants’ own confidence was low. Confidence also affected heuristic strategies: confident others prompted participants to compromise and copy social information more often, rather than to stick with their initial estimates. We discuss how following confident others when uncertain can improve decision-making, but also leaves people vulnerable to sources of misinformation.

articles.title: Disrupting social media habits: a one-week detox produces enduring reductions in use and automaticity
articles.authors: Tim van Timmeren; Suhaavi Kochhar; Mariek Magdalena Petra Vanden Abeele; Sanne de Wit
articles.abstract: This randomised controlled trial examines if a one-week social media abstinence intervention can reduce social media use by lowering automaticity of and craving for social media use. Participants motivated to reduce their social media use were assigned to an immediate one-week detox (N = 50) or a waitlist control condition (N = 64). Using a combination of smartphone usage logging and weekly surveys, we found that the detox produced significant reductions in social media use (d = 0.51), automaticity (d = 1.10), and craving (d = 0.58) one week post-detox relative to the waitlist group. Exploratory mediation analyses provided suggestive evidence that automaticity partially mediated the detox's effect on social media use. Furthermore, baseline automaticity predicted self-reported vulnerability to slips of action during the detox, i.e. spontaneous attempts to open removed apps. Pooling data from both groups after each had completed the detox (N = 108), we found that the reductions persisted across the three-week follow-up and that social media use remained below baseline at a six-month follow-up in a subsample (N = 46). The detox also shifted participants' subjective relationship with social media, increasing perceived control and reducing self-reported mindlessness, without changing how much they liked it or considered it purposeful. Together, these findings suggest that for those who want to cut back, taking a short break is an effective way to disrupt social media habits and restore a sense of control.

articles.title: The influence of attention on visual statistical learning and vice versa: Insights from frequency-based grouping as revealed by EEG frequency tagging
articles.authors: Elena Greatti; Davide Crepaldi
articles.abstract: The human brain readily captures regularities in the environment. It is not clear, however, whether and how this skill—statistical learning—interacts with attention. We addressed this issue by leveraging neural entrainment, the synchronization of brain activity with statistical structure. In Study 1, we asked whether sensitivity to a frequency-based regularity, created by embedding low-frequency items among higher-frequency items, competes for attentional resources with a concurrent task. Participants viewed structured or random visual streams while performing a 3-back color matching task. Neural entrainment emerged only for structured streams, demonstrating sensitivity to the frequency structure. Improvement in the concurrent task, indexed by decreasing response times, unfolded more slowly when structure was present, suggesting that detecting statistical regularities drew attention away from the 3-back color matching task. In Study 2, we tested the reverse connection—whether taxing attention with a more difficult task impairs the neural tracking of statistical structure. We compared entrainment during an easier color-change detection task and a more difficult 3-back color matching task. We observed no detectable effect of attentional load on neural entrainment. These findings reveal an asymmetric relationship between attention and frequency-based statistical learning: detecting structure imposes a modest attentional cost on a concurrent behavioral task, whereas the online neural tracking of regularities appears to be unaffected by increased attentional demands.

articles.title: Quality of Life and the Case for Consent-Based Psilocybin Access – Questions on the Regulatory Framework and Cost
articles.authors: Janis Ancans
articles.abstract: Legal access to psilocybin almost always requires a medical diagnosis first, usually treatment-resistant depression (TRD) or severe PTSD, as though informed consent alone was not sufficient. This article makes two connected arguments. Extending the autonomy argument already accepted for terminally ill patients, competent adults who understand the potential benefits and risks of a psilocybin experience should be able to choose it for reasons of psychological wellness or existential anxiety relief, not only because a clinician has certified a qualifying illness, a right the legal literature calls “cognitive liberty”. Just as important, the cost of access is not fixed; it reflects the regulatory framework under which psilocybin is provided. No jurisdiction has yet completed medicines authorisation pathway; the furthest-advanced clinical programme, Compass Pathways' COMP360, met its Phase 3 primary endpoint and reported six-month durability data for TRD by July 2026, and its developer has since signalled an annual cost close to that of esketamine nasal spray, USD 50,000–65,000, or roughly USD 17,000–22,000 per dose. Meanwhile, Australia's narrower authorised-prescriber legal route for TRD, using GMP-manufactured but unregistered psilocybin, already costs AUD $20,000 per course. Three distinct non-medical routes cost far less. Truffles in the Netherlands, sold under food law with no diagnosis and no supervision required, and Colorado and Oregon's state-licensed psilocybin services, which require no diagnosis but do involve a supervising facilitator, cost up to $3,000 per session. Removing the diagnosis requirement while leaving this cost structure untouched risks replacing the regulatory barrier with the wealth-based one, unless expanded access is paired with public subsidy. Article also briefly reviews the safety evidence, the political origins of psilocybin's scheduling, and the double standard in how its risks are treated. A Canadian case illustrates the institutional and regulatory framework dysfunction, a dying man denied psilocybin for existential relief while approved for medical assistance in dying within weeks, before the article closes with policy recommendations addressing both access and funding.

articles.title: Trauma Processing Therapy: A Precision-Weighted Approach to Memory Reconsolidation
articles.authors: Jiemi Ardian; Matius Dimas Reza Dana Ismaya; Ines Damayanti Octaviani; Yosefina Sonia Christya Kartika
articles.abstract: Trauma-focused therapy yields positive outcomes for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, many individuals do not experience total remission, and symptoms may recur. This might happen because extinction-based learning could maintain the initial fear memory, which can be reactivated at a later time. Inquiry into memory reconsolidation has not yet revealed the requisite circumstances for consistently updating a memory. This article puts forth Trauma Processing Therapy (TPT), a theoretical approach founded on predictive processing. TPT interprets traumatic memories as proxies for extremely precise, multidimensional models that are resistant to corrective information. The fundamental theory suggests that persistent alteration relies on precisely calibrated prediction error while memory is in a pliable state. The process is adaptive and operates as a closed loop. The therapist recognises the primary affective state, evokes and amplifies a corrective emotional anticipation, activates both together, and then observes changes in relation to the initial recollection. When a cycle fails, the protocol distinguishes two types of responses. If the response is inert, this indicates the need to change the corrective approach, while if the response is resistant this indicates the need to challenge the ideas that are hindering progress. A composite clinical vignette is presented to demonstrate the application of the approach in practice. It is not evidence for the effectiveness of TPT or for reconsolidation being achieved. Structured investigations, meticulous analyses and ongoing assessments are essential to confirm these predictions. TPT is an applied theoretical proposition; its therapeutic utility and proposed mechanisms remain to be empirically tested.

articles.title: Recruiting families into preventive parenting programs: Messaging responses and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents
articles.authors: Katie Qintan Lin; Emma Marshall; Danhua Zhu; John W Toumbourou; Elizabeth Westrupp
articles.abstract:
Objective: Preventive parenting programs can reduce child mental health risks, but equitable reach requires effective recruitment. Little is known about how recruitment messaging can engage underserved culturally diverse families while retaining broad population appeal. We compared responses to recruitment messaging and participation barriers among Chinese-heritage and White parents. 
Methods: Parents of children aged 2-5 years (100 Chinese-heritage, 101 White) in English-speaking Western countries were recruited online. Participants rated six parenting program recruitment messages based on the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Goal-Directed Behaviour, Norm Activation Model, their combination, or Chinese cultural values (guan and harmony), and nine participation barriers. Mixed-effects regression models examined participation likelihood, perceived program usefulness, and barrier relevance by ethnicity and message/barrier type. 
Results: Chinese-heritage parents reported lower participation likelihood and perceived program usefulness, and higher average barrier relevance than White parents. Ethnicity-by-message interactions were not significant; descriptively, guan was highest rated among Chinese-heritage parents and Goal-Directed Behaviour among White parents, while the combined behavioural theory message was highly rated across groups. Ethnicity-by-barrier interactions were significant: Chinese-heritage parents rated seven of nine barriers as more relevant compared to White parents. Lack of time was most relevant among Chinese-heritage parents; concern about data security was most relevant among White parents, although its relevance did not differ significantly between groups. 
Conclusions: Findings extend research on cultural adaptation to recruitment, and highlight the need to balance cultural responsiveness with broad appeal while addressing families’ differing barriers to participation.

articles.title: Computational Affective Science
articles.authors: Kate Petrova
articles.abstract: Affective science is the interdisciplinary study of phenomena such as emotions, moods, attitudes, and stress responses, which together make up a large part of the forces that energize and direct behavior. The field has developed rich theories of motivation and emotion and generated an impressively large empirical literature on affect in human and nonhuman behavior. In this paper, I argue that the field is now well poised for a systematic turn toward computational modeling. I begin by explaining what computational modeling is, trace how it has transformed neighboring disciplines, and lay out what affective science stands to gain from it. Many computational models of affect and motivation already exist, but this work remains scattered across fields that rarely speak to one another. I review this work across three interrelated domains: (1) models of specific, circumscribed affective phenomena; (2) applied models in computational psychiatry and affective computing; and (3) broader theoretical models that aim to explain what affect is and how it arises. Finally, I outline a vision for the new field of Computational Affective Science—one that transcends the boundary between affect and cognition in pursuit of a cumulative science of motivated behavior.

articles.title: Be a Meditator Today: Testing Identity-Based Message Framing for Meditation in a Digital Field Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract:
Objectives. Brief in-app messages are commonly used to prompt meditation, but little is known about which message features influence engagement. Drawing on the reasoned action approach and research on self-identity, this study tested whether framing meditation as an identity (“Be a meditator today”) rather than a behavior (“Meditate today”) increases engagement, and whether any effect depends on prior engagement.

Methods. In a randomized field experiment on Spotify, 3,000 U.S. adults who had recently listened to a popular meditation teacher received one of two in-app messages that differed only in identity versus behavior framing. Outcomes were message click-through and listening to the teacher’s content during the treatment period, analyzed by intent to treat. Logistic regression tested moderation by prior listening.

Results. Click-through did not differ between conditions (8.2% vs. 8.2%; difference = −0.05 percentage points, 95% CI [−2.03, 1.92]). Identity framing did not increase listening during the treatment period (Mann–Whitney U = 1,106,605, p = .313; mean difference = 1.26 min, 95% CI [−5.72, 8.24]). Prior listening (median split) did not moderate the effect of framing (interaction OR = 0.93, 95% CI [0.55, 1.56], p = .77).

Conclusions. Identity-based framing did not increase engagement, even among an audience for whom the meditator identity was plausible. Consistent with the reasoned action approach, changing a message’s grammatical form without changing the beliefs it makes salient may offer little leverage over behavior.

articles.title: Reading Minds Beyond the Eyes: Conceptual Knowledge Structures Mental State Perception
articles.authors: Maryam Bin Meshar; Jonathan B. Freeman
articles.abstract: The ability to infer others’ mental states is central to understanding human behavior. Across four studies (total N = 827), we examined how facial information and perceivers’ conceptual knowledge structure mental-state inferences. In Study 1, participants identified 60 complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eye region removed or isolated eye regions, demonstrating the importance of information beyond the eyes. Study 2 showed that mental states believed to co-occur were perceived as more similar in facial appearance. Crucially, perceivers’ idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own facial-similarity judgments even after accounting for associations shared across participants. Studies 3 and 4 extended this correspondence from perceptual similarity to categorical identification: conceptually associated states were more likely to be confused with one another, both for standardized posed expressions and for naturalistic, unposed faces. On trials involving misidentification, participants’ unique conceptual associations predicted which incorrect mental-state label they selected above and beyond shared conceptual structure. Together, these findings suggest that inferring mental states from faces depends on both distributed facial information and the conceptual organization perceivers bring to the task. More broadly, they identify individual differences in conceptual knowledge as a source of systematic variation in how people read minds from the same facial expressions.

articles.title: Data-driven recommendations for increasing reliability and validity in measures of infant word recognition
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Virginia A. Marchman; Heidi A Baumgartner; Claire Augusta Bergey; Mika Braginsky; Federico Giovannetti; George Kachergis; Jess Mankewitz; Stephan Meylan; Ben Prystawski
articles.abstract: Children’s early word recognition is both an important phenomenon in its own right and a key index of early language more broadly. A central paradigm for measuring word recognition in young children is the looking-while-listening paradigm (LWL), which tracks eye movements to the referent of a word as a measure of online language comprehension. Yet the analytic and design choices for LWL vary widely, and the consequences of these choices have rarely been investigated at a large scale. Here we use data from Peekbank, a repository of LWL data from studies with almost 4000 children (6 months--5 years), to search for analytic and design decisions that maximize the reliability and validity of LWL measures. Analytic recommendations include using long analytic windows for computing accuracy and avoiding baseline correction. We also find little or no benefit from excluding children or trials with low data. The recommended combination of analytic choices increased reliability (intra-class correlations and test-retest correlations) by approximately .20 and validity (correlations with productive vocabulary) by .07. Effects were generally consistent across age, but gains for reliability were more substantial than for validity. Design recommendations include building experiments with a minimum of 10 target trials per child per condition and matching stimuli for animacy. We hope that these recommendations lead to improved and unified standards for the measurement of children’s word recognition in the LWL paradigm.

articles.title: Use of communication channels in 2x2 strategic games
articles.authors: Veronica Boyce; Avidit Acharya; Michael C. Frank
articles.abstract: How do we use language to coordinate with each other? This question is of interest both from the cognitive science of language perspective as well as the game theory perspective. Here we attempt to bridge the gap between the empirical tradition of studying language use for coordination in reference games with the theoretical and analytic framework of game theory. We conducted a series of 5 real-time online experiments where pairs of participants were matched to play a sequence of 40 2x2 games together (total N=616). Across the experiments, we varied the exact structure of trials, but all experiments involved trials with reward structures modeled on Prisoner’s Dilemma (PD) and Bach or Stravinsky (BoS). We manipulated the presence or absence of a chat interface as a between-pairs manipulation. Despite low levels of use of the communication channel, we found slight differences in outcome between the chat and nochat groups, where pairs who could communicate were slightly more likely to reach coordinated beneficial outcomes in BoS games. In contrast to the predictions of rational actors, participants in both chat and no-chat conditions generally aligned on both cooperating rather than both defecting in PD. Overall, we were limited in our ability to discern the role of communication channels in game strategies due to low uptake in using the communication channels when available.

articles.title: Lost in Mentalization? Revisiting the Mentalizing Construct
articles.authors: Moria Laznik Strauss; Julieta Piastro Behar
articles.abstract: Abstract: Over the past three decades, mentalization theory has captured the imagination and curiosity of clinicians, researchers, educators, and professionals across a broad range of disciplines. Alongside its growing influence, questions concerning the definition and measurement of mentalizing as a target construct have remained a recurring theme in literature. This raises two related questions: what are we measuring when we assess mentalizing, and what is the empirical basis for conceptualizing it as a four-dimensional construct? The four-dimensional formulation assumes that four distinct dimensions can be identified and measured, that their polarities form meaningful continuum, that balance and imbalance can be defined, and that the dimensions together form a coherent psychological structure. We propose distinguishing between the assessment of the mentalization theory and of mentalizing itself as a target construct. Adopting a curious, not-knowing stance, we revisit these assumptions and invite further consideration of the architecture and measurement of the mentalizing target construct.

articles.title: Daily life evidence against the general relieving function of conspiracy beliefs
articles.authors: Armin Gyarmati; Levente Rónai; Gábor Orosz; Lili Jakobovits; Péter Krekó; Bertalan Polner
articles.abstract: Conspiracy theories are assumed to provide psychological relief, reducing anxiety and uncertainty in the short term, at the cost of longer-term harms. Nevertheless, the temporal dynamics of conspiracy beliefs have rarely been investigated in naturalistic settings. Here, we tested whether fluctuations in conspiracy mentality are associated with changes in anxiety and sense of coherence in everyday life, using experience sampling data collected in a Hungarian (N = 77, Nobs = 2,905) and a pre-registered representative U.S. sample (N = 200, Nobs = 10,609). In both samples, we found moderate to strong evidence against a general association of conspiracy mentality with anxiety and sense of coherence across multiple timescales spanning from hours to weeks. However, among older adults, increases in conspiracy mentality were followed by lower anxiety and a higher sense of coherence, while individuals reporting no psychiatric diagnosis also benefited in terms of reduced anxiety. Together, these findings challenge the notion that conspiracy beliefs function as a universal buffer against anxiety and uncertainty, while the exploratory analyses point towards boundary conditions requiring further investigation.

articles.title: Acoustic and visual cues to lexical stress interact with semantic predictions in Spanish lexical stress perception
articles.authors: Floris Cos; Matteo Maran; Hans Rutger Bosker; Esther Janse; Lieke van Maastricht
articles.abstract: Next to acoustic cues, lexical stress can be communicated visually through the timing of beat gestures. This study investigated for the first time how auditory and visual lexical stress cues are weighted in meaningful sentences. Minimal stress pairs of Spanish verb forms (clasiFIco, “I classify” vs. clasifiCÓ, “(s)he classified”) were embedded in sentence contexts that biased towards either member of the pair. Stress was manipulated acoustically along a continuum, and visually by aligning a beat gesture to the penultimate or last syllable. Native listeners selected the pronoun (yo “I” or ella “she”) they felt fit best with the sentence. Listeners were sensitive to acoustic cues, as indicated by both responses and response times. While gesture alignment did not significantly affect pronoun selection, response times were shorter when the gesture matched the semantic context bias. This study thus shows that in full sentences, congruent (vs. incongruent) gestural timing affects word recognition.

articles.title: Rethinking Smartphones and Sleep: A Fine-Grained Within-Person Analysis of Evening Smartphone Use and Sleep
articles.authors: Fenne große Deters; Katharina Salo; Jan A. Häusser; Anne Milek
articles.abstract: Inadequate sleep is a public health concern associated with adverse health and well-being outcomes. Evening smartphone use is frequently cited as a potential contributor, prompting widespread recommendations to avoid it. However, rigorous evidence to support these recommendations is limited. Using device-based smartphone use data and experience sampling data collected over 10 days, we examined within-person associations between evening smartphone use and five self-reported sleep-related outcomes: shuteye time, sleep latency, sleep duration, difficulty to fall asleep, and sleep quality. We examined these associations in two samples (N = 184 and N = 185) to test replicability. To investigate robustness and temporal dynamics, we assessed smartphone use across four equal-length time windows covering different segments of the evening. Across both samples and all time windows, greater-than-usual evening smartphone use was consistently associated with earlier shuteye time. Associations with the other sleep-related outcomes were less consistent, with most estimates indicating no significant relationship. Overall, our findings align with previous intensive longitudinal research that has likewise found little evidence of concerning associations between evening smartphone use and sleep. Our results challenge the assumption that evening smartphone use is inherently harmful to sleep and underscore the need to reconsider blanket recommendations to avoid it.

articles_hidden.title: From comparison to transformation: studying minds that learn from machines
articles_hidden.authors: Francesca Bertacchini; Eleonora Bilotta
articles_hidden.abstract: For seventy years, minds and machines have been studied by comparison: can machines model, imitate or outperform us? In bounded domains this comparison has saturated, and machines now produce certified knowledge that no person can inspect; a complete Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem runs to 13.5 million lines. We argue that the object of study must move from the performance gap to the change in minds that learn from machines. We propose Reverse Cognition: a search for faithful, explicitly limited representations through which a person can acquire a certified structure and keep it once the machine is withdrawn. In the public formalization, only 5.7% of the theorems beneath the four steps of the human proof belong to a single step. We define audit criteria for representational routes, machine operations that could make such objects followable, predictions that separate appropriation from offloading, and a study sequence to test them.

articles_hidden.title: Equanimity and Eating-Disorder Vulnerability: Dissociating Psychological Dispositions from Approach–Avoidance Biases
articles_hidden.authors: Nassim Elimari; Claire El Jor; Yoann Julliard; Yoann Durand; Quentin Hallez; Catherine Juneau; Valentin Flaudias; Rebecca Shankland
articles_hidden.abstract: Equanimity, a regulatory quality cultivated through mindfulness practices, refers to the capacity to maintain a balanced mental stance toward pleasant and unpleasant experiences without being automatically driven toward attachment or avoidance. Although theoretically expected to weaken the influence of evaluation on behavior, empirical evidence linking equanimity to observable behavioral dynamics remains limited. The present study examined associations between equanimity, eating-disorder vulnerability, and automatic approach–avoidance tendencies toward food cues. Participants (N = 215) completed self-report measures of equanimity, eating-disorder risk, mindful eating, self-compassion, experiential avoidance, and body acceptance. A subset of 183 participants additionally completed a food-specific approach/avoidance task using stimuli varying in hedonic value. At the dispositional level, equanimity was associated with lower eating-disorder vulnerability and experiential avoidance, and greater self-compassion, body acceptance, and mindful eating. These associations were largely driven by the even-minded state of mind facet of equanimity, whereas hedonic independence showed weaker, more circumscribed relationships with eating- and body-related variables. Behavioral analyses revealed faster avoidance of low-hedonic than high-hedonic food cues, but neither equanimity nor its facets predicted reaction times or moderated hedonic effects on approach/avoidance dynamics. These findings suggest that while equanimity is associated with reduced eating-disorder vulnerability at the trait level, its regulatory role may not manifest in the earliest motor expressions of food-related action tendencies. Instead, equanimity may primarily influence later stages of regulation, such as the interpretation, tolerance, or behavioral management of emerging impulses. However, this interpretation warrants further exploration in experienced meditators, as equanimity in the general population may differ from that cultivated through prolonged contemplative practice.

articles_hidden.title: Why the Mix Matters - Exploring the Dynamics of Polysubstance Use
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Uhl; Anastasiya Bunina; Birgit Ursula Stetina
articles_hidden.abstract: A widespread form of recreational drug use is known as polysubstance use, which involves consuming two or more psychoactive substances within a short period of time. In addition to the desired effects, such as intensifying or prolonging the high, or counteracting unpleasant effects, polysubstance use also entails risks. To provide polysubstance users with user-centered measures to support health promotion and safer-use, a differentiated understanding of the diverse forms of this consumption practice is required. In an online cross-sectional study, recreational drug users (N= 649) were asked about sociodemographic data and their consumption behavior, with a particular focus on polysubstance use. A hierarchical cluster analysis was performed to identify different types of polysubstance users. The clusters obtained were then tested for diversity using chi-square tests. The cluster analysis revealed three polysubstance use groups that differed in the frequency of mixed use, underlying motivations, and the presence of risk-minimizing strategies. The study showed that consumers who use multiple substances do not constitute a homogeneous group and differ in various characteristics. Taking these individualities and diversities into account must serve as the basis for health promotion to address consumers in a targeted manner.

articles_hidden.title: The Mint Scale: A Fresh Validation of the Multimodal Interoception Questionnaire and Comparison to the MAIA, BPQ and IAS
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Ana Neves; Emma Lucy Benn; Maisie Bennett; Giulia Poerio
articles_hidden.abstract: Interoception, the sensing of the body's internal state, is an important component of homeostatic and allostatic regulation with wide-ranging implications for mental and physical health, yet its measurement is hindered by tools with conceptual and psychometric issues. To address these limitations, we developed and validated the Multimodal Interoception Questionnaire (Mint). In Study 1 (N=559), a comprehensive item pool using a novel "modality-by-context" framework was generated and then reduced using psychometric network analysis. In Study 2 (N=737), we validated the Mint in an independent sample, establishing its structure,  comparing its predictive power against established interoception questionnaires (MAIA-2, BPQ, IAS), and across a wide range of clinical and cognitive outcomes. This rigorous process yielded a 33-item scale with a stable hierarchical structure comprising three metaclusters (Interoceptive Deficit, Interoceptive Awareness, Visceroception) and 11 distinct facets. The Mint demonstrated superior criterion validity, consistently outperforming existing scales in predicting outcomes tied to altered bodily perception, including alexithymia, ADHD, autism, and somatic symptom clusters. The Mint offers a psychometrically robust and nuanced measure of self-reported interoception that integrates and extends existing scales, providing researchers and clinicians with a practical and readily usable tool to investigate the role of bodily sensations in health and disease.

articles_hidden.title: Confirmatory feedback adds little to serial dependence, whereas error feedback reverses it
articles_hidden.authors: Yael Shamir-Bercovich; Shir Angel; Aihua Chen; ADAM ZAIDEL
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceptual decisions are shaped not only by current sensory input but also by recent experience. Serial dependence exposes an internal brain process that biases current decisions toward previous ones, even in the absence of feedback about their correctness. When available, feedback on one’s choices is an external factor that also shapes subsequent decisions. However, how correct- and incorrect-choice feedback separately affect choice-history biases relative to no feedback, and how these effects vary across individuals and modalities, remains unclear. Here, we compared the effects of serial dependence with or without trial-by-trial feedback on perceptual decisions regarding vestibular or visual self-motion stimuli, and examined how they relate to autistic traits. Seventy healthy adults performed a two-alternative forced-choice heading discrimination task with visual or vestibular cues (separately), under two conditions: with feedback indicating whether each choice was correct or incorrect, and without feedback. Without feedback, significant choice repetition was seen in both modalities. Surprisingly, on average correct-choice feedback did not enhance the choice repetition effect; rather it remained similar in magnitude. By contrast, incorrect-choice feedback led to a large, opposite effect – choice switching – which was stronger for vestibular cues. Thus, only error signals, not confirmatory signals, substantially modulated serial dependence. Choice repetition in the no-feedback vestibular condition correlated significantly with autistic traits. This relationship was not observed when feedback was provided. The similarity in choice repetition following correct-choice feedback vs. no feedback was more pronounced in individuals with high autistic traits, and suggests that positive serial dependence (without feedback) may reflect an internal assumption that one’s decisions were mostly correct.

articles_hidden.title: The built environment and mental health: a neurobiological framework for risk and resilience
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Cleo Valentine; Lara Gregorians; Uemee Jung; Anjan Chatterjee; Esther Sternberg; Agustin Ibanez; Harris Eyre; John Kounios; Nicklas Berild Lundblad
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health is shaped by multiple factors, including the built environment. As urbanisation increases, urban living has been associated with higher rates of depression, anxiety and psychosis, although the evidence remains predominantly associative. Here, we synthesise epidemiological, neuroimaging and environmental research into a six-domain framework for understanding how built-environment qualities may relate to mental health risk and resilience. The domains comprise Safety and Accessibility, Cognitive Load and Environmental Complexity, Multisensory Integration, Emotional Valence, Social Connection, and Naturalness and Biophilia. We link these domains to neural, physiological, cognitive, emotional and social pathways, and outline methods for testing them across environmental, experiential and neurobiological levels. The framework provides a structure for developing more precise and testable hypotheses about how specific characteristics of the built environment may influence mental health and resilience.

articles_hidden.title: From exposure to experience: Viewing nature activates parahippocampal cortex while subjective reports of naturalness are associated with reduced lateral occipital activity
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Lara Gregorians; Cleo Valentine; Uemee Jung; Pablo Fernandez Velasco; Eva Zita Patai; Fiona Zisch; Hugo Spiers
articles_hidden.abstract: The benefits of incorporating elements of nature into architectural settings to improve wellbeing and cognition has been explored in numerous studies. However, the brain dynamics associated with exposure to natural elements in architecture and the subjective experience of nature in such settings remains unclear. Here we examined fMRI data recorded while participants watched first-person-view movies of architectural spaces that varied in the extent to which they included natural elements (green space or water). These natural elements were decorrelated across movies from the other aspects of the movies, such as subject rated valence and layout complexity. This design also permitted dissociation of the visual presence of natural elements (exposure) from the subjective sense of connectedness to nature they elicit (experience), dimensions that are frequently conflated in the extant literature. Movies were rated for a range of qualities from the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX), which revealed that perceived connectedness to nature was partly dissociable from the presence of green space, water, luminance, layout complexity and valence of the spaces. Videos of spaces with nature were associated with increased activity in areas associated with scene processing and navigational affordances (parahippocampus, and occipital regions). Connectedness to nature was associated with a reduction in activation in bilateral lateral occipital regions. These results provide new insights into how natural features and the sense of naturalness in architectural spaces may affect brain regions that are linked to visual processing and affordances.

articles_hidden.title: Multi-study exploration across controlled indoor spaces: Initial evaluation of the feasibility and sensitivity of the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX)
articles_hidden.authors: Isabelle Sjovall; Uemee Jung; Cleo Valentine; Emre Yavuz; James Moultrie; Lucia Bussell; Lola Artiles San Juan; Jiang Zhu; George Joseph; John Draper
articles_hidden.abstract: People spend much of their lives in built environments, yet methods for evaluating how these environments are experienced remain limited. This research reports the first multi-study application of the NeuroDesign/NeuroArchitecture Index (NDIX), a multidimensional measure of environmental experience, and examines whether it is sensitive to meaningful differences between standard and environmentally enriched indoor spaces. Study 1 used a randomised repeated-measures crossover design in which 42 participants evaluated a standard quiet room and an enriched redesign of the same space. Study 2 (N = 40) evaluated standard and enriched innovation environments using complementary repeated-measures (n = 19) and independent-groups (n = 20 per group) comparisons. In both settings the instrument was administered in full in a single short session. In Study 1, NDIX Overall was higher in the enriched environment than in the standard environment (dz = 1.83), with higher scores across all six domains after false discovery rate correction and an equivalent effect in both presentation orders. Internal consistency was good for NDIX Overall (α = .87 and .89) but variable across domains (α = .40 to .77). Free-text descriptions of the most salient change centred on green plants, artwork and layout. Study 2 reproduced the pattern, with NDIX Overall higher in the enriched environment both within participants (dz = 2.50) and between independent groups (d = 1.90). The findings indicate that the NDIX is practical to administer and sensitive to meaningful environmental variation, while further psychometric evaluation is required across populations, environmental contexts, and more subtly differing settings.

articles_hidden.title: Meaningfulness shapes strategic memory use
articles_hidden.authors: Luzi Xu; Surya Gayet; Andre Sahakian; Chris Paffen; Stefan van der Stigchel
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent studies show that working memory for meaningful real-world objects can far exceed traditional capacity limits (~4 items) under experimental conditions where items are briefly presented. In everyday life, however, information often remains accessible, and observers freely choose how much to remember now and how much to inspect later. Under such unconstrained conditions, people typically memorize only 1–2 items at a time, far below maximum capacity. Here, we asked how meaningfulness influences strategic memory use during unconstrained memory-guided behavior. Using a copying task that allows for reinspections of the display, we compared meaningful real‑world objects with meaningless (novel‑but‑realistic) objects matched on low‑level visual features. Across two experiments, meaningfulness increased memory use, boosting it from ~2.5 items (meaningless objects) to ~3.8 items (meaningful objects) per sampling. Thus, the advantage of real‑world objects extends beyond capacity: it changes how people balance memory use against re-sampling of information in natural behavior.

articles_hidden.title: Memorability as an Emergent Property: How Representational Structure Creates Apparent Intrinsic Effects
articles_hidden.authors: Dyllan Simpson; John Wixted; Timothy F. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: Some pictures, videos, faces, voices, and words are reliably remembered better than others, a phenomenon known as memorability. This has been widely interpreted as reflecting a stable, intrinsic property of the stimuli themselves. Here we argue that this consistency is better explained by the relational structure of the stimulus sets used to measure memorability, rather than as an intrinsic property of the items. Using simulations with a global matching model of recognition memory, we show that apparent intrinsic memorability emerges naturally from distinctiveness — how dissimilar an item is from others in a given set of encoded images — without any stimulus-intrinsic mechanism. In behavioral experiments, we demonstrate that manipulating the similarity structure of image sets can invert memorability rankings, making previously memorable images forgettable and vice versa. We also show that features previously identified as intrinsically memorable (such as “body-part related”) are the most representationally distinctive features in standard databases, explaining their memorability. To address these large variations in distinctiveness we created a new image set that reduced variability in representational distinctiveness, and found it significantly diminishes all feature-memorability relationships. These findings suggest that memorability is not a fixed attribute of items themselves, but an emergent property of which items are distinctive within the context, with implications for how we attribute stable psychological properties to stimuli more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: Functional Structural Detachment: How Useful Perceptual Structure Carries Value Across Contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Jacek Rogala; Marek Kuś; Beata Bajno; Shabnam Kadir
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract forms can move us. A securely fixed sculpture can still look ready to fall and make us uneasy. Why does this visual pattern affect us when nothing can fall? We propose that what perceivers evaluate is often not an object as such but structure in sensory signals that carries information about the state and properties of objects and events. Deformation can indicate stiffness, the relation between mass and support can indicate stability, and visual expansion can signal approach. When such information matters for what a perceiver does or for what happens to them, the structure that carries it acquires evaluative weight. This structure is often available before the object is identified, and under poorer conditions: in the periphery, at a distance, in poor light, and for objects never seen before. Responding to it lets perceivers prepare to act early, at the price of responding wherever the structure appears, including in objects they cannot identify.
Some evaluative influence can remain when the information no longer serves its original use, which we call functional detachment (FD), and it can appear in new objects or events that preserve the same informative structure, which we call structural transfer. Together, they define functional structural detachment (FSD). The influence persists in part because a structure with little use in one context remains important in others.
FSD predicts that evaluative influence transfers further when the structure has a broad functional history, having been useful across many different situations, even when perceivers detect it equally well. We describe experiments that separate this account from salience, processing fluency, simple association, and the valuation of current consequences.
Art provides a limiting case: abstract forms can retain structures that were informative about objects and events elsewhere, and these structures can continue to affect us even when their original source and practical role have become remote.

articles_hidden.title: Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA): Nodal Variance Decomposition and Coefficient Gamma for Psychometric Networks
articles_hidden.authors: César Huerta-Huacchahuilca; Jano Ramos-Diaz
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychometric network analysis faces a foundational methodological divide: while rejecting the latent common-cause assumption, applied studies evaluate composite score reliability using classical common-cause coefficients (α, ω) or substitute metric precision with bootstrap partition frequencies (bootEGA), incurring indirect reliability induction under REGEMA guidelines and violating AERA/APA/NCME testing standards. We introduce Reliability Exploratory Graph Analysis (rEGA), an analytical framework grounded in support-constrained maximum likelihood refitting (K̂_refit) and the Neumann–Markov resolvent operator (Q = [I − Ω]⁻¹). rEGA establishes the Law of Conservation of the Nodal Triad, partitioning standardized item variance into Within-Community Communality (hᵢ²), Inter-Community Bridging Variance (βᵢ²), and Markov Nodal Uniqueness (ψᵢ²), such that hᵢ² + βᵢ² + ψᵢ² ≡ 1.000. From this decomposition, rEGA defines a purity-weighted adjacency matrix (A^rEGA), Within-Community (Γ_c) and Total Network (Γ_t) reliability coefficients, and the Graph Standard Error of Measurement (SEM^raw). Across a Monte Carlo simulation of 97,200 datasets (972 conditions), rEGA-Leiden outperformed Walktrap, Louvain, and Parallel Analysis in dimensionality recovery (87.65% vs. 64.81%–71.32%), eliminated ℓ₁-shrinkage bias (RMSE_ψ = .035), classified core, bridge, and noise nodes with 86.8%–99.4% accuracy, and yielded unbiased reliability estimates (Bias_Γ = −.007) immune to lexical doublet inflation. Multi-sample validation on the AAQ-II (N = 3,200) and DASS-21 (N = 2,751) demonstrated that the Nodal Triad Leakage Criterion (β̄² > h̄²) rules out spurious over-fragmentation while distinguishing noisy items (A1) from transdiagnostic bridges (D2, S3, S6) with high cross-sample invariance (r > .93). Separating structural validity from score error, rEGA prevents ad hoc scale pruning and reconciles network psychometrics with international measurement standards.

articles_hidden.title: MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder: A Qualitative Analysis of Patient Experiences of Change
articles_hidden.authors: Christina Chwyl; Malena Donas; Angelica Spata; Gabriella Gatto; Akeesha Simmons; Kim Hoffman; M. Kati Lear; Brian Pilecki; Jenna LeJeune; Jason B Luoma
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: This study represents the first qualitative analysis to explore experiences of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) for people with social anxiety disorder. 

Method: Following two MDMA (midomafetamine) sessions, participants (N = 20) completed semi-structured interviews of their treatment experiences. Team members derived themes pertaining to what aspects of treatment participants felt contributed to therapeutic benefit through reflexive thematic analysis.  

Results: Five themes were identified: 1) Healing Catalysed by Gently Facing Difficult Experiences (sub-themes: Moving from Criticism to Curiosity and Compassion; Enhanced Capacity to Access and Process Emotions); 2) Meaning Making through Broadened Perspectives of Self and Others (sub-themes: Clarity on the Origins of Distress; Deeper Understanding of Authentic Self; Interconnectedness and Oneness); 3) From Intellectual to Felt Knowing through Embodied States (sub-themes: Emotional Experiencing and Release; Feeling Safe and at Ease with Oneself); 4) Learning New Relational Patterns through Vulnerable Self-Expression; and 5) MDMA Experiences as Anchor for Ongoing Self-Discovery. 

Conclusion: Overall, participants felt that MDMA in the context of a safe therapeutic container facilitated them facing, deeply feeling and embodying emotions, which catalysed new insights and healing. By feeling more connected and at ease with themselves and with others, participants gained the motivation to show up authentically in their relationships.

articles_hidden.title: What You Notice Moves You More: Self-Reported Arousal Follows Noticed Changes in Paced Breathing
articles_hidden.authors: Norman A. S. Farb; Kyle Logie; Rose Amir Pour
articles_hidden.abstract: Does bodily change shape self-reported arousal only when it is noticed? In the Breath Change Awareness Task, participants breathe with a visual pacer or follow it by vision alone, report whether its pace changed, and rate arousal. After four development studies (Prolific adults and undergraduates, N = 579), we report a preregistered laboratory study (N = 206) with verified breathing. Arousal followed noticed changes more steeply than missed ones, with or without breathing, and in most studies noticed effects scaled with a change's size beyond the reported direction. In Study 5, missed changes moved arousal up to a third as much although breathing tracked the pacer closely, and a noticed breathed change moved arousal 1.8 [1.3, 2.7] times as much as one followed by vision alone, though not detectably in the online Study 4. Ratings partly followed the preceding detection report. Self-reported arousal mainly follows noticing; breathing adds to it.

articles_hidden.title: No evidence that overnight sleep improves associative inference
articles_hidden.authors: Johannes Wibroe; Shane Lindsay
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep can help preserve learned associations, but evidence that it also helps people draw new inferences from them is mixed. We tested both outcomes in the same task, comparing performance after a 12-hour overnight interval with performance after a daytime interval of the same length. In an online experiment, participants learned overlapping object pairs (A–B and B–C) and were tested on them immediately and again after the delay. Only at the delayed test were they asked to infer the relationship between objects linked through the shared item (A–C). We analysed accuracy and response times using Bayesian multilevel models. Memory for the learned pairs declined in both groups, and inference accuracy remained close to chance. Inferences were more likely to be correct when participants also recognised both of the pairs needed to make them. Overall, the results gave no clear evidence of an overnight benefit for memory or inference and were consistent with participants retrieving and combining the learned pairs at test.

articles_hidden.title: Appetitive Food Rewards and Cognitive Flexibility: Reward Transitions, Voluntary Task Switching, and Individual Differences
articles_hidden.authors: Beatrice Lomeo; Joseph M Orr
articles_hidden.abstract: Motivation shapes how people allocate cognitive control, including whether they persist with a current task or flexibly switch to another.
