articles_hidden.abstract: ata from repeated-measures experiments (e.g., response time data, electrophysiological data) can show systematic changes in outcomes over time, so-called (temporal) trends. When analyzing experimental effects between conditions, different trends per condition can cause the experimental effect to vary with time, for example, to decline over the course of the experiment. Previous research has shown that ignoring time-varying effects in an analysis can influence results and distort conclusions, whereas explicit modeling yields more informative results and valuable insights into the underlying (psychological) processes. This article provides a systematic introduction to modeling trends and time-varying experimental effects in experimental data, accounting for fixed trends (across participants) as well as random (person-specific individual) trends. We consider different modeling approaches: exact parametric models, linear or polynomial growth curve models, generalized additive mixed models (GAMMs) and the recently proposed random-effects-expectation-maximization (RE-EM) trees. We provide an overview of these different modeling approaches and compare their performance and data requirements in two simulation studies based on the characteristics of realistic data from a cognitive response time experiment. We conclude that polynomial models suffice for simple smooth trends. Otherwise, GAMMs and RE-EM trees are more suited. We derive specific recommendations for their application from our results, provide a tutorial on how these models can be applied in the open source software R, and explain how their results can be interpreted along with presenting annotated R-code. We conclude with a recommended workflow on how a combination of the investigated methods can help researchers better understand time-varying effects.

articles_hidden.title: Diverse Mechanisms of Adaptive Variability in Human Behavior
articles_hidden.authors: Janne Reynders; Tom Verguts; Senne Braem
articles_hidden.abstract: Adaptive variability in behavior is crucial when environments promote unpredictability, yet its underlying cognitive mechanisms remain poorly understood. Volatile and adversarial environments can elicit variability by abrupt rule switches and explicitly reinforcing variable choices, respectively; however, literature lacks paradigms, computational models, and data to investigate and compare how (human) agents address such challenges. We introduce a novel hide-and-seek paradigm and use computational modeling to disentangle five candidate cognitive mechanisms of variability: stochastic choice, fast reinforcement learning, action-frequency-based memory, sequence-frequency-based memory, and episodic memory. Across three experiments (N = 290), we show that participants flexibly increased learning rate in volatile environments, but stochasticity, action-frequency-based memory, and reliance on episodic memory in adversarial environments. For the first time, these findings uncover that adaptive variability is not a unitary phenomenon but instead emerges from the flexible recruitment of multiple cognitive mechanisms as environmental demands intensify.

articles_hidden.title: A comparison of state-of-the-art signal classification  algorithms in a locked-in end-user with a tactile P300 based BCI in long-term home-use
articles_hidden.authors: Maria Pfeiffer; Philipp Ziebell; Claudia Tröger; Wolfgang Tröger; Sebastian Halder; Thomas Giesler; Andrea Kübler; Matthias Eidel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) constitute a last resort of communication for people with severe motor impairments. To date, several potential improvements of BCI-related hardware and software components have been investigated, for instance, classification algorithms for brain signals such as electroencephalography (EEG). These efforts focused on laboratory work with healthy participants. However, this is not representative for real-life conditions of potential motor-impaired end-users with diseases like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Our study compares state-of-the-art classification approaches on a real-life dataset of an end-user with ALS and a tactile P300-based BCI, which was obtained in long-term home-use.
Approach: We applied state-of-the-art classification approaches, including Shrinkage Linear Discriminant Analysis (ShrinkLDA) and Riemannian Geometry Classifiers (RGC). Moreover, we tested effects of different calibration scenarios (i.e., amount of training data, time between calibration) and spatial filtering (using xDawn). These variations were compared to the classification results of a commonly used Stepwise Linear Discriminant Analysis (SWLDA). As a criterion for sufficient performance, we defined an accuracy of >70% (based on prior work). 
Main results: SWLDA could be outperformed, but without spatial filtering via xDawn, no classification algorithm was able to allow for sufficient independent home-use (with accuracies ranging between 33% to 66%; SWLDA: 59%). The addition of spatial filtering via xDawn notably improved classification results for all classifiers, with the best performance achieved by RGC_xDAWN and ShrinkLDA_xDAWN (both 72% accuracy; SWLDA_xDAWN: 70%).
Significance: This is the first study comparing classifiers on a large set of tactile P300-based BCI data obtained from an end-user in his own home. Of the state-of-the-art classifiers (established with healthy participants), only two reached slightly beyond a performance accuracy of >70%. Future work can build on our findings (e.g., implement spatial filtering) and further investigate the consequences of real-life conditions for potential end-users (e.g., disease characteristics, hardware and software optimization, environmental factors).

articles_hidden.title: Beyond comorbidity: cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety as a stress-related self-maintaining system in aging.
articles_hidden.authors: Matias M. Pulopulos; Maxime Bertoux; Fabien D'Hondt; Rudi De Raedt
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, and psychological disorders (particularly late-life depression and anxiety) are highly prevalent in aging, often co-occur, and predict each other over time. Importantly, stress exposure across the lifespan and dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system (ANS), the two main biological stress systems, are considered causes and exacerbators of these age-related conditions. However, the stress-to-disease pathway in aging has proven hard to demonstrate consistently, and health trajectories vary widely between individuals. We argue that this partly reflects how the problem has been modeled, with cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological health problems in aging studied as separate downstream outcomes of stress and HPA axis and ANS dysregulation. We review and propose several neurocognitive, neurovisceral, and psychophysiological mechanisms that may explain how these three conditions form a mutually reinforcing system. Importantly, these mechanisms also feed back onto the HPA axis and ANS, disrupting their circadian and context-sensitive regulation. We identify middle adulthood as the period in which these reciprocal influences strengthen. Moreover, we propose that the domain first affected and individual reserve shape the health trajectory and which conditions co-occur. In this framework, we argue that stress-system dysregulation in aging should be considered both a cause and a consequence of cognitive decline, cardiometabolic dysfunction, depression and anxiety, forming a self-maintaining loop that may provide a systems-level mechanism through which stress-related multimorbidity contributes to trajectories commonly associated with accelerated biological aging.

articles_hidden.title: When actions speak louder than words: Maintaining verbally instructed movement representations is driven by action imagery rather than verbal rehearsal
articles_hidden.authors: Carla Czilczer; Markus Martini; Pierre Sachse; Stephan Frederic Dahm
articles_hidden.abstract: When imagining actions based on verbal movement instructions, maintaining an evolving mental representation across successive instructions is important. We examined this process from a working memory perspective, asking whether maintenance of verbally instructed action imagery depends on verbal working memory or can be sustained by action imagery-related processes. In an adapted Final Position Judgment Task (FPJT), participants imagined three to six successive movements from listening to standardized movement instructions. They then judged whether an image of a human figure matched their imagined final position. Participants completed the FPJT in two conditions, once in baseline and once while repeating a syllable aloud to prevent verbal rehearsal. This articulatory suppression increased errors but performance remained above chance, suggesting that performance was not reducible to verbal rehearsal. Converging with this, FPJT errors were associated with visuospatial, but not verbal, working memory, with these associations not varying by FPJT condition. Articulatory suppression reduced reported verbal rehearsal and action imagery quality, whereas in both conditions, more than 80% reported visual rehearsal of instructed body parts to maintain imagery. Visual rehearsal was associated with fewer errors in baseline. Our results suggest that maintaining verbally instructed action imagery in the FPJT relies on action imagery-related visual rehearsal and visuospatial working memory, with verbal rehearsal playing a supporting role. Given that FPJT performance also covaried with mental body rotation and mental paper folding performance, the FPJT appears suitable for assessing action imagery ability.

articles_hidden.title: When risks add up: Cumulative psychosocial adversity and suicidality in an online sample of Latvian adults: a preregistered cross-sectional study
articles_hidden.authors: Edmunds Vanags; Marta Gēbele; Liene Sīle; Liene Konošonoka; Artjoms Soboļevs; Sibilla Krūmiņa; Elmars Terauds; Maris Taube; Romija Krezina
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Latvia has one of the highest suicide rates in the European Union, yet evidence on the psychosocial and mental health correlates of suicidality among Latvian adults remains limited. This preregistered study examined correlates of a composite suicidality outcome.

Methods: A cross-sectional nonprobability online survey of Latvian adults was conducted between May 2025 and February 2026. Of 1,018 participants in the analytic sample, 1,006 had an observed primary outcome. Measures included depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), workplace bullying (NAQ-R), alcohol use (AUDIT), and adapted UK Biobank items on trauma exposure, psychiatric symptoms, and substance use. The primary outcome was a binary composite of suicidal ideation or attempt in the past 12 months, or a lifetime suicide attempt. Hypotheses were tested using multivariable and hierarchical logistic regression, with estimates pooled across 20 multiply imputed datasets and complete-case sensitivity analyses. The protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8hjea).

Results: Lifetime suicide attempts were reported by 7.6% of participants (76/999), suicidal ideation by 61.9% (614/992), and self-harm by 21.4% (212/992). The composite outcome was present in 34.5% (347/1,006). Clinically significant depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 ≥ 10) were associated with higher odds of suicidality (OR = 5.33, 95% CI 3.97–7.16, p < .001). Compared with low perceived social support, strong support was associated with lower odds after adjustment for age, gender, and employment status (OR = 0.15, 95% CI 0.08–0.28, p < .001). Adding mental health variables to the demographic model increased Nagelkerke's R² from .095 to .345. Participants with four or more prespecified risk factors had higher odds than those with zero or one (OR = 21.53, 95% CI 11.07–41.88, p < .001). Complete-case analyses yielded broadly consistent results.

Conclusions: Depressive symptoms, lower perceived social support, and cumulative psychosocial adversity were associated with suicidality. The cross-sectional design and nonprobability sampling limit generalisability to the Latvian adult population. Nationally representative longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporal associations.

articles_hidden.title: Face and eye gaze in preterm and full-term preschoolers during face-to-face interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Rowena Van den Broeck; Laura Tibermont; Lisa Gistelinck; Niilo Valtakari; Bieke Bollen; Els Ortibus; Gunnar naulaers; Bart Boets; Roy S Hessels
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Preterm birth has been linked to atypical social development and difficulties with social orientation similar to those observed in autism. A fundamental component of social interaction is adequate gaze toward an interaction partner’s face and eyes. Preterm individuals have been reported to display atypical social gaze patterns, characterized by more frequent but shorter looks toward faces. Methods: We compared looking times to the face, as well as eyes versus mouth during face-to-face interactions in preterm (N = 45) and full-term (N = 29) five-year-olds, using a video-based eye-tracking set-up. Secondary, we examined number of dwells and mean dwell duration. Each child participated in four interaction tasks, including silent looking at their mother, silent looking at a female stranger, and a positive and negative conversation with their mother. Results: No statistically significant group differences were found between preterm and full-term children in percentage of total dwell times to either the face or the eyes, however small differences were observed with preterm children showing less dwells per minute with longer mean durations than full-term children. We observed a marginal effect of interaction partner, with children spending proportionately more time gazing at their mother’s face than at a stranger’s face. Conclusion: Preterm and full-term five-year-olds showed no differences in total social gaze to the face and the eyes of their interaction partner during face-to-face interactions, although subtle differences were observed in other gaze measures. Speculatively, these findings may reflect a developmental catch-up in social orientation following initial delays in infancy. Alternatively, advances in neonatal medical care, including infant-directed interventions in the neonatal intensive care unit, may have been successful in improving social gaze after preterm birth. Given the context-dependent and individual nature of gaze behavior, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Future longitudinal studies employing consistent methodological approaches are needed to investigate how social gaze develops over time following preterm birth.

articles_hidden.title: Psychodiagnostic Markers and Linguistic Indicators of Psychological Capital: A Theoretical Model of Complementarity Within the Structural-Functional Paradigm of Human Capital
articles_hidden.authors: Dmytro Melnychuk; Oleksii Sabadukha; Iryna Kovalenko
articles_hidden.abstract:
Rapid epochal transformations call for rethinking human capital as a dynamic emergent entity with a complex architecture of endogenous components: educational-competence, health, social, and psychological capital. Within this architecture, psychological capital (PsyCap) acts as a cross-cutting moderator that determines the extent to which the educational-competence core is converted into socio-economic outcomes. This raises the significance of PsyCap psychodiagnostics while exposing the limitations of reflective self-report instruments, which capture momentary self-assessments and remain vulnerable to social desirability bias.
The article aims to substantiate the integration of linguistic indicators into PsyCap assessment and to develop a matrix model mapping the four HERO components (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) onto classes of linguistic indicators. Drawing on systemic, structural-functional, and interdisciplinary approaches, the study uses construct validity criteria to frame linguistic indicators as external correlates within the nomological network of PsyCap.
The model matches hope with achievement and goal-setting markers, efficacy with markers of confidence and control, resilience with register flexibility and reduced negative affect, and optimism with positive-emotional and forward-oriented language. Linguistic indicators cannot replace standardized instruments; rather, they constitute a complementary data source, provided that linguistic and cultural adaptation, control of socio-economic confounders, and ethical safeguards against profiling are ensured. The study builds a conceptual bridge between psychodiagnostics and psycholinguistics and outlines a pathway toward the culturally adapted operationalization of PsyCap assessment in Ukrainian psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles_hidden.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Impact of Exergames on Cognition in Midlife and Older Age: A Bayesian Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Cognitive decline in older adulthood is a pressing global concern, prompting growing interest in scalable behavioral interventions. Exergames, which integrate physical activity and cognitively engaging tasks, have emerged as a promising approach to support cognitive health in aging. This Bayesian meta-analysis synthesizes 48 studies (181 effects; N = 2,605) on adults aged 50+, published up to May 31, 2024, examining the impact of exergames on cognition. Without adjustment for publication bias, exergames showed a small positive effect across cognitive domains. However, after adjusting for publication bias, the evidence for an overall effect was inconclusive, and no cognitive domain (i.e., attentional control, processing speed, working memory, cognitive flexibility, global cognition) showed more than anecdotal evidence for an effect. Moderator analyses provided no evidence that effects differed by factors such as age, population type (e.g., non-clinical vs. clinical), or intervention characteristics (e.g., exergaming modality, type of product, session frequency and duration, or intervention duration). These findings call for more rigorous, standardized, and well-powered trials to establish whether exergames benefit cognition in middle-aged and older adults.
